name: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders

clinicalPearls: A peptic ulcer is a break in the mucosa larger than 5 mm that extends into the submucosa; more than 90% of patients with the classic dyspepsia symptom complex have no ulcer, and many patients with true ulcers are asymptomatic (Harrison 22e p.2514, p.2522).

Burning/gnawing epigastric pain typically occurs 90 minutes to 3 hours after eating in duodenal ulcer and is relieved by food or antacids; pain that wakes the patient between midnight and 3 A.M. is the most discriminating symptom (about two-thirds of DU patients), though it also occurs in roughly one-third with non-ulcer dyspepsia (Harrison 22e p.2522).
In gastric ulcer the pain may instead be precipitated by food, and nausea and weight loss are more common than in duodenal ulcer (Harrison 22e p.2522-2523).

H. pylori and NSAIDs are the two dominant risk factors (US odds ratios about 3.7 and 3.3); idiopathic and non-Hp/non-NSAID ulcers are rising as H. pylori prevalence falls (Harrison 22e p.2518, p.2522).
Gastric ulcers can be malignant and must be biopsied at discovery; duodenal ulcers are almost never malignant (Harrison 22e p.2518).

NSAID toxicity correlates poorly with symptoms: over 80% of patients with serious NSAID-related complications had no preceding dyspepsia, and even 75 mg/day of aspirin can cause serious ulceration, so no NSAID dose is completely safe (Harrison 22e p.2520-2521).

About two-thirds of PUD patients have no abdominal pain, and up to 87% of those with NSAID-induced disease present with a complication without prior symptoms; more than 50% of ulcer hemorrhages occur without warning (Harrison 22e p.2522).

Antral-predominant H. pylori gastritis predisposes to duodenal ulcer, whereas corpus-predominant gastritis predisposes to gastric ulcer, atrophy, and ultimately gastric carcinoma (Harrison 22e p.2519-2520).

Endoscopy is the most sensitive and specific test; it detects an ulcer in fewer than 30% of patients presenting with dyspepsia, allows biopsy to exclude malignancy and detect H. pylori, and barium studies are now rarely used (Harrison 22e p.2523).

A fasting serum gastrin above ten times normal strongly suggests Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, but two-thirds of ZES patients have gastrin levels that overlap with commoner causes; a secretin-stimulated rise of 120 pg/mL or more within 15 minutes is over 90% sensitive and specific (Harrison 22e p.2535-2536).

Suspect gastrinoma with ulcers in unusual locations (second part of duodenum or beyond), refractory or recurrent ulcers, ulcers with complications, or ulcers without H. pylori or NSAID use; about 25% of gastrinomas arise in MEN 1 (Harrison 22e p.2534-2535).

Stress-related mucosal injury (Cushing's ulcer after head injury, Curling's ulcer after burns) histologically lacks inflammation and H. pylori, so 'gastritis' is a misnomer; bleeding typically appears 48-72 h after the insult with mechanical ventilation and coagulopathy as key risk factors (Harrison 22e p.2536).
harrison.pathophysiology: Ulcers result from an imbalance between mucosal aggressive factors (gastric acid secreted by parietal-cell H+,K+-ATPase, pepsin from chief cells) and mucosal defense/repair (a preepithelial mucus-bicarbonate-phospholipid layer, epithelial restitution and tight junctions, and a subepithelial microvascular bed), with prostaglandins, nitric oxide, and mucosal blood flow central to protection. H. pylori, a gram-negative microaerophilic urease-producing rod, colonizes gastric mucus, causes chronic active gastritis in nearly all infected individuals, and produces frank ulceration in only 10-15%; virulence factors include urease (generating ammonia), CagA delivered by a type IV secretion system from cag-PAI-positive strains, VacA, and adhesins. Antral-predominant gastritis raises acid and promotes duodenal ulcer, whereas corpus-predominant pangastritis lowers acid and favors gastric ulcer and carcinoma. NSAIDs injure mucosa both systemically (COX-1 inhibition depletes protective prostaglandins) and topically (weak acids that become trapped and ionized intracellularly), with neutrophil adherence to the gastric microcirculation initiating injury; H. pylori and NSAIDs act as independent and synergistic risk factors. In Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, autonomous gastrin secretion from a neuroendocrine tumor drives acid hypersecretion, parietal-cell hyperplasia, ulceration, esophagitis, and diarrhea (Harrison 22e p.2514-2521, p.2534).
additionalDifferentials: Functional (non-ulcer/essential) dyspepsia, including postprandial distress syndrome and epigastric pain syndrome (commonest cause of upper abdominal discomfort)
infectionMimics: Infectious causes of large gastric folds mimicking Menetrier's disease (CMV, histoplasmosis, syphilis, tuberculosis)
nonInfectiousMimics: Drug/toxin-induced ulceration (bisphosphonates, clopidogrel, glucocorticoids combined with NSAIDs, potassium chloride, mycophenolate, chemotherapy, immune checkpoint inhibitors, crack cocaine)
Menetrier's disease and gastric polyposis presenting as large gastric folds
additionalInvestigations: Upper endoscopy with biopsy (most sensitive/specific; biopsy gastric ulcers to exclude malignancy)
H. pylori testing: rapid urease biopsy test, histology, culture (allows susceptibility testing)
Noninvasive H. pylori tests: 13C-urea breath test and stool monoclonal antigen test (both >95% sensitivity/specificity); serology cannot distinguish active from prior infection
Fasting serum gastrin (two occasions) when ZES is suspected
Secretin stimulation test (rise >=120 pg/mL at 15 min) and gastric pH/acid analysis for gastrinoma
Serum calcium, parathyroid hormone, prolactin, and pancreatic polypeptide to screen for MEN 1 in gastrinoma patients
Tumor localization imaging and somatostatin-receptor-based studies for gastrinoma
Screening blood/urine for surreptitious aspirin/NSAID use in refractory H. pylori-negative ulcers
redFlags: Sudden severe generalized abdominal pain with a board-like, rigid abdomen suggesting perforation
Tarry stools or coffee-ground emesis indicating gastrointestinal bleeding; tachycardia/orthostasis indicating hypovolemia
Persistent pain no longer relieved by food/antacids and radiating to the back suggesting posterior penetration (pancreas)
Early satiety, vomiting of undigested food, and a succussion splash suggesting gastric outlet obstruction
Weight loss, anorexia, or new dyspepsia at age 60 or older warranting endoscopy before empiric therapy
Ulcers in unusual locations, refractory/recurrent ulcers, or multiple ulcers prompting evaluation for gastrinoma
harrison.prognosis: Eradication of H. pylori reduces duodenal ulcer recurrence by more than 80%, and improving sanitation has steadily lowered ulcer incidence, surgery rates, and physician visits over the past decades. Complications still carry meaningful mortality: GI bleeding (the commonest, ~15% of patients) has a 30-day mortality of about 2.5-10% and is more frequent in those over 60; perforation occurs in about 6-7% of patients with 30-day mortality over 20%; gastric outlet obstruction is the least common (1-2%). Approximately 15,000 deaths per year in the US are attributed to complicated PUD. For gastrinoma, overall 5- and 10-year survival is about 62-75% and 47-53%; complete resection or negative laparotomy yields survival over 90%, while hepatic metastasis drops 5-year survival below 20% (Harrison 22e p.2514, p.2516, p.2522-2523, p.2536).
pitfalls: Treating dyspepsia as PUD: abdominal pain has poor predictive value and most dyspeptic patients have no ulcer, so empiric assumptions can miss alternative diagnoses.
Relying on symptoms to gauge NSAID risk: serious complications usually occur without preceding dyspepsia.
Failing to biopsy a gastric ulcer to exclude malignancy.

Misinterpreting an elevated fasting gastrin: PPIs, hypochlorhydria/achlorhydria, pernicious anemia, H. pylori, renal insufficiency, retained antrum, and G-cell hyperplasia all raise gastrin, and PPIs must be stopped (about 7 days, bridged with an H2 antagonist) before ZES testing to avoid false positives.
Assuming serology proves active H. pylori infection, when it cannot distinguish current from prior infection and is unreliable for follow-up.
Abruptly stopping PPIs in gastrinoma patients, which can precipitate severe acid-related complications.
Calling stress-related mucosal injury 'gastritis' despite the absence of inflammation, or labeling endoscopic erythema as gastritis without histology.
harrison.severityClassification: PUD severity is framed clinically by the presence and type of complication: uncomplicated ulcer versus bleeding (commonest, ~15%, 30-day mortality ~2.5-10%), perforation/penetration (~6-7%, 30-day mortality >20%; DU penetrates posteriorly into pancreas, GU into left hepatic lobe), and gastric outlet obstruction (1-2%, may be inflammatory/reversible or fixed scar). For gastrinoma, prognosis is stratified by resectability and metastatic burden rather than a formal stage in this chapter (Harrison 22e p.2522-2523, p.2536).
